title: Return to Their Lands
summary: In the twenty-sixth year, the people of the Nephites return to their own lands with their families, animals, remaining provisions, and possessions. They return to lands northward and southward.
characters: People of the Nephites and their families
locations: Their own lands and possessions in the land northward and the land southward

explicit_facts.text: The people of the Nephites returned to their own lands in the twenty-sixth year, each man with his family, flocks, herds, horses, cattle, and belongings.
They took their remaining provisions, grain, gold, silver, and precious things to their lands and possessions northward and southward.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Family groups travel with livestock and carried possessions.
unspecified_visual_details: Specific routes, clothing, architecture, and the travelers' appearances.

narration.text: the people of the Nephites did all return to their own lands
both on the land northward and on the land southward.

prohibited_inventions: Do not add named individuals or a distinct group of settlers.
Do not imply that every traveler follows the same route.

title: Land Granted for Peace
summary: Lands are granted to robbers who covenanted to keep the peace and wished to remain Lamanites.
characters: The robbers who covenanted to keep the peace

explicit_facts.text: The people granted lands according to the number of robbers who had covenanted to keep the peace and wished to remain Lamanites.
The grants allowed them to subsist through their labors, and peace was established throughout the land.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A land allocation may be depicted with people receiving or occupying land.
unspecified_visual_details: The grant ceremony, exact lands, and any officials or witnesses present.

narration.text: they did establish peace in all the land

prohibited_inventions: Do not invent a formal ceremony or specific terms beyond the text.

title: Order and Prosperity
summary: The people prosper under equitable laws, and Gidgiddoni, judge Lachoneus, and appointed leaders are credited with establishing peace.

explicit_facts.text: The people prospered, and there was great order in the land with laws formed according to equity and justice.
Nothing hindered continual prosperity except transgression.
Gidgiddoni, judge Lachoneus, and appointed leaders had established peace.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Leaders may be shown together in a civic setting.
unspecified_visual_details: The leaders’ appearance, meeting place, and specific laws.

narration.text: there was great order in the land
who had established this great peace in the land

prohibited_inventions: Do not depict specific legislation or attribute spoken words to the leaders.

title: Cities and Roads
summary: New cities are built, old cities repaired, and highways and roads connect places as the twenty-eighth year passes in continual peace.

explicit_facts.text: Many cities were built anew and many old cities repaired.
Highways and roads were made between cities, lands, and places.
The twenty-eighth year passed, and the people had continual peace.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Construction and connected roads can be shown as a broad view of the land.
unspecified_visual_details: City designs, building materials, workers, and the exact course of roads.

narration.text: many highways cast up, and many roads made
the people had continual peace

prohibited_inventions: Do not depict a specific city or named builders.

title: Disputes and Pride
summary: In the twenty-ninth year, disputes and pride arise among the wealthy; the land has many merchants, lawyers, and officers.

explicit_facts.text: Disputes began among the people in the twenty-ninth year, and some became proud and boastful because of great riches, leading to persecutions.
There were many merchants, lawyers, and officers in the land.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A public gathering with disputing people may illustrate the reported social conflict.
unspecified_visual_details: The subject of the disputes and any particular individuals involved.

narration.text: there began to be some disputings among the people
many merchants in the land

prohibited_inventions: Do not invent specific arguments or identify particular persecutors.

title: Ranks by Wealth and Learning
summary: People become distinguished by wealth and access to learning; some are proud and retaliatory while others endure affliction humbly.

explicit_facts.text: People were distinguished by ranks according to riches and chances for learning; some were ignorant through poverty and others received great learning through riches.
Some were proud; others were humble. Some returned railing for railing, while others received railing and persecution without reviling in return and were penitent before God.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Contrasting groups may be shown in separate portions of one social setting.
unspecified_visual_details: The individuals’ identities, exact wealth, education, and specific words exchanged.

narration.text: distinguished by ranks, according to their riches
would not turn and revile again

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The account describes social inequality and differing responses to persecution.
prohibited_inventions: Do not supply dialogue for the railing or depict a specific act of persecution.

title: The Church Broken Up
summary: Inequality grows, and by the thirtieth year the church is broken up throughout the land except among a few converted Lamanites who remain steadfast.

explicit_facts.text: Great inequality developed, and by the thirtieth year the church was broken up throughout the land except among a few Lamanites converted to the true faith.
Those Lamanites remained firm, steadfast, and immovable, diligently keeping the Lord’s commandments.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A contrast between divided people and a small steadfast group can convey the stated difference.
unspecified_visual_details: The setting of any gathering and the appearance or number of the converted Lamanites.

narration.text: there became a great inequality in all the land
they were firm, and steadfast, and immovable

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The text identifies the few converted Lamanites as an exception to the church’s breakup.
prohibited_inventions: Do not portray the church’s breakup as a specific meeting or confrontation.

title: The Cause of Iniquity
summary: The account attributes the people’s iniquity and loss of peace to Satan’s influence, pride, and temptation; by the start of the thirtieth year they are wicked.

explicit_facts.text: The account says Satan had great power to stir the people to iniquity and pride and tempt them to seek power, authority, riches, and worldly things.
Satan led the people’s hearts to iniquity, and they enjoyed peace for only a few years.
At the commencement of the thirtieth year, the people were in a state of awful wickedness after being carried about by the devil’s temptations.

reasonable_visual_inferences: Use narration over a visual of the people, without depicting a literal supernatural event.
unspecified_visual_details: Any visible form or appearance of Satan, and the specific acts of iniquity.

narration.text: Satan had great power
they were in a state of awful wickedness

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Satan’s influence is described as the cause of iniquity, not as a narrated visible appearance.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show Satan or depict temptation as a literal visible supernatural scene.

title: Willful Rebellion
summary: The people knowingly rebel against God. Lachoneus’s son governs in his father’s place that year.

explicit_facts.text: The people knew God’s will because they had been taught, and they willfully rebelled against God.
In that year Lachoneus’s son filled his father’s seat and governed the people.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The governing son may be shown in a civic setting; the rebellion need not be shown as a separate action.
unspecified_visual_details: The son’s appearance and the place where he governed.

narration.text: they did wilfully rebel against God
did govern the people that year

prohibited_inventions: Do not conflate Lachoneus the father with the son who governed.

title: Testimony and Anger
summary: Men sent forth preach and testify boldly among the people throughout the land. Many people, chiefly chief judges, those who had been high priests, and lawyers, are angry with those who testify.
characters: Those who had been high priests
locations: Among the people in all the land

explicit_facts.text: Men inspired from heaven were sent forth and stood among the people in all the land, preaching and testifying boldly of the people's sins and iniquities, redemption, Christ's resurrection, death, and sufferings.
Many people were exceedingly angry because of those who testified; the angry included chiefly chief judges, those who had been high priests, and lawyers. All the lawyers were angry.

reasonable_visual_inferences: A man addressing a group of people can depict the preaching.
Some listeners may appear angry, without assigning an office or past role based on appearance.
unspecified_visual_details: The men's appearances, the setting's precise location, and the listeners' clothing and gestures.

narration.text: preaching and testifying boldly of the sins and iniquities of the people,
and they did testify boldly of his death and sufferings.

doctrinal_or_story_notes: Christ's resurrection, death, and sufferings are subjects of testimony, not events occurring in this scene.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict Christ appearing or assign invented words to the men.
Do not identify particular listeners as judges, former high priests, or lawyers solely by invented visual markers.

title: Judges Secretly Kill Witnesses
summary: The law requires a governor’s signed condemnation for a death sentence, yet judges secretly put some witnesses of Christ to death without the governor’s knowledge, contrary to law.

explicit_facts.text: No lawyer, judge, or high priest could condemn anyone to death without a condemnation signed by the governor.
Judges secretly put to death many who testified of Christ, and the governor learned of their deaths only afterward.
Putting anyone to death without the governor’s authority was contrary to the laws of the land.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The secret killings may be conveyed conservatively without showing injury or gore.
unspecified_visual_details: Where the killings occurred, how they were carried out, and the victims’ identities.

narration.text: were taken and put to death secretly by the judges
this was contrary to the laws of the land

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The passage reports the deaths and the unlawful secrecy; it does not describe the physical manner of death.
prohibited_inventions: Do not show wounds, blood, or a method of killing; do not depict the governor witnessing the deaths.

title: Complaint Against the Judges
summary: A complaint reaches the governor in Zarahemla, and the judges are brought before a judge to answer for their crime under the law.
characters: The judges accused of condemning the prophets

explicit_facts.text: A complaint was brought to the governor against judges who had unlawfully condemned the Lord’s prophets to death.
The judges were taken before a judge to be tried according to the law given by the people.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The accused judges may be shown before a judge in a legal proceeding.
unspecified_visual_details: The complainants’ identities, the hearing’s appearance, and its outcome.

narration.text: a complaint came up unto the land of Zarahemla
brought up before the judge to be judged

prohibited_inventions: Do not invent testimony, a verdict, or a sentence.

title: A Covenant Against Justice
summary: Almost all the lawyers and high priests gather and unite with the kindreds of judges who are to be tried. They enter a covenant to combine against righteousness, destroy the people of the Lord, and deliver those guilty of murder from justice.
characters: Kindreds of the judges who were to be tried

explicit_facts.text: The judges who were to be tried had many friends and kindreds; almost all the lawyers and high priests gathered and united with the judges’ kindreds.
They entered a covenant described as given and administered by the devil, to combine against all righteousness.
They combined against the people of the Lord and covenanted to destroy them and deliver those guilty of murder from impending justice.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The gathering can be shown as people assembled together.
unspecified_visual_details: The gathering place, clothing, individuals’ appearances, and manner of entering the covenant are not described.

narration.text: did gather themselves together
And they did enter into a covenant one with another
to deliver those who were guilty of murder from the grasp of justice

doctrinal_or_story_notes: The devil’s role is stated, but no visible appearance is described.
The judges and those guilty of murder are not stated to be present at the gathering.
prohibited_inventions: Do not depict the devil or invent an oath, ritual, or spoken words.
Do not identify the judges as those guilty of murder or depict a rescue or destruction not narrated here.

title: Plot to Establish a King
summary: The conspirators defy the law and their country’s rights, covenanting to destroy the governor and establish a king over the land.

explicit_facts.text: The conspirators set at defiance the law and the rights of their country.
They covenanted to destroy the governor and establish a king so the land would be subject to kings rather than remain at liberty.

reasonable_visual_inferences: The conspirators may be shown gathered in deliberation.
unspecified_visual_details: The governor’s identity, the proposed king’s identity, and any planned method or timing.

narration.text: to destroy the governor
to establish a king over the land

prohibited_inventions: Do not depict an attack, the governor’s death, or a king being installed; none occurs in the supplied verses.
